newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Budget - The leaked winners and losers.
newsitem.headline: Australia Budget - The leaked winners and losers.

text.p: Australia's conservative Liberal/National government is scheduled to release its budget for the year to June 30, 1998 at 7.30 p.m. (0930 GMT) on Tuesday.
This is the government's second budget.
In recent weeks, various measures in the budget are believed to have been leaked to various media groups.

Economists surveyed earlier on Tuesday forecast the government would set an underlying deficit target of around A$2.5 billion in 1997/98, based on outlay reductions and revenue changes of about $1.0 billion to A$1.5 billion.
The government has projected an A$8.5 billion underlying deficit for the year to June 30, 1997 and has previously said it wanted to achieve underlying balance in 1998/99.
The combined leaked measures are as follows;

* The government is expected to forecast 3.5 percent to 3.75 percent GDP growth in 1997/98, 2.0 percent employment growth and an unemployment rate of 8.0 percent by June 1998 - (The Australian, May 12.)

* Health spending is expected to be cut by A$1.6 billion over four years, with A$700 million from new prescription drug pricing arrangements targetting the chronically ill and the elderly - (The Australian, May 12.)

* The budget would contain a new tax rebate aimed at low and middle income earners, which would cut tax payments on interest earned from savings accounts, costing A$1 billion a year. The funding for this would come from the dumping of Labor's tax cut/pension payment planned for 1997/98 that would have cost about A$4.5 billion. The compulsory employee contribution to
superannuation schemes would also be abandoned - (Sydney Morning Herald, May 11.)
* People approaching the retirement age of 65 would be offered a A$20,000 bonus to keep working until age 70 - (The Telegraph, May 10.)
* Child-care payments for mothers staying at home rather than working would be cut back, saving A$400 million a year - (The Sydney Morning Herald, May 9.)

* A new capped tax rebate scheme would be introduced to replace the abolished infrastructure bond programme. The government may also clamp down on dividend washing, raising an extra A$400 million a year - (The Australian Financial Review, May 12.)
